newsitem.title: CHILE: Russian space probe too deep to recover.
newsitem.headline: Russian space probe too deep to recover.

text.p: Chile's navy has discovered the location of the failed Russian Mars '96 space probe in the Pacific but the ocean's depth means the wreckage will be impossible to recover, a government official said on Tuesday.

"The information that the navy has given me, which is confirmed, is that at least part of it fell into the Pacific Ocean about 1,600 miles (3,000 km) west of Santiago between Easter Island and the mainland," Deputy Foreign Minister Mariano Fernandez said.

The wreckage of the remains of the probe, which was carrying seven ounces (200 grams) of plutonium, is lying on the ocean floor at a depth of around 19,700 feet (6,000 meters) which will make salvage efforts futile, he said.
"The depth means that all access is impossible..."

Although most of the probe was likely to have been destroyed on re-entry, U.S. scientists said it was probable the rocket's four batteries containing the radioactive plutonium fell to the bottom of the ocean. The plutonium was inside two landers and two penetrators that were designed to withstand the heat and stress of landing on Mars.
The probe carried 22 instruments from 20 nations.
Fernandez said that Chile would continue investigations with atomic energy experts and the Russian government into the danger to rich fishing grounds in the area from radioactivity.

"There is enough plutonium there for a massive contamination of an entire aquatic ecosystem," Chilean environmental leader Manuel Baquedano said on Monday. He said the area in the South Pacific between Easter Island and the Chilean mainland contains tuna, mackerel and bonito and trawlers from around the world fish there.

Russian officials said the four batteries, each about the size of a roll of film, were designed to withstand great heat and great stress on impact on the planet Mars. But Baquedano and other environmentalists said the water pressure at that depth could be too much for any man-made object to withstand.
"We face the danger that our entire industrial and small-scale fishing stocks could be contaminated," biologist Bernado Reyes said on Monday.
The ill-fated Mars 96 probe crashed into the Pacific on Sunday after a booster rocket misfired, preventing it from breaking out of Earth's gravity.
The satellite will deliver scientific equipment, fuel, oxygen, water, food, instruments and parcels to the three members of Mir's crew. It is expected to dock 48 hours after being launched.
Russia is still smarting from the embarrassing loss of its Mars-96 mission at the weekend.

The Mir crew -- cosmonauts Valery Korzun and Alexander Koleri and U.S. astronaut John Blaha -- had been due to be relieved in mid-December. But cash problems meant the launch of the next crew, including a German, was postponed to February.
Blaha and his two Russian colleagues have been aboard Mir station since September 19. Four Mir launches have been held up this year because of money troubles in the Russian space industry.
